title: API 570 Training in Newark: Piping Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 570 exam prep online for North Jersey piping inspectors: Bayway unit piping, harbor dock and transfer lines, CUI in salt air and freeze-thaw winters.
h1: API 570 Piping Inspector Exam Prep for Newark and the New York Harbor Shore
html:
API 570 exam prep for piping inspectors from Newark Bay to Perth Amboy

Piping is what ties North Jersey's industrial shore together. Process lines run through the Bayway refinery's units in Linden, steam and utility lines cross between neighbouring companies in the same complex, and dock and transfer lines join the tank farms at Bayonne, Carteret and Perth Amboy to ships, barges and the products pipelines that end at the harbor. An API 570 inspector here may spend the morning on a refinery pipe rack and the afternoon on a marine loading header.

Atlantis NDT's API 570 course prepares you for the API 570 Piping Inspector examination. It is self-paced and online with instructor Q&A: you begin when you enrol, fit study around shifts and turnaround work, and send questions about B31.3 clauses or API 570 calculations as they arise. There is no Atlantis classroom in Newark. The American Petroleum Institute sets the eligibility rules, administers the exam in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification.

Unit piping in a complex where five companies share a fence line

Bayway is unusual because its piping does not all belong to one owner. An economic study prepared by NJIT for the New Jersey Business & Industry Association, using 2023 data, counts five firms in the complex: the Phillips 66 refinery, Infineum's additive operations, Nexpera's acid regeneration business, the Linden Cogeneration plant and a Sunoco LP fuel terminal, with the cogeneration plant selling steam to Phillips 66 and Infineum under long-term contracts. Wherever a line crosses from one company to another, someone has to decide whose inspection programme the circuit belongs to, where it ends and who keeps its thickness history.

Inside the refinery, EIA's 2026 capacity report lists catalytic cracking, high-pressure reforming, solvent deasphalting and hydrotreating behind 275,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation. Those services cover most of the RP 571 mechanisms on the API 570 Body of Knowledge for the 2027 windows:

Piping serviceRP 571 mechanisms on the Body of Knowledge
Crude, vacuum and cracking unit hot linesSulfidation; erosion and erosion-corrosion where velocity or catalyst is involved
Crude unit overhead and reformer effluent linesHydrochloric acid corrosion
Hydrotreater effluent and sour water linesSour water corrosion (acidic)
Amine treating linesAmine stress corrosion cracking
Steam and condensate returnBoiler water and steam condensate corrosion
Caustic and stainless chemical serviceCaustic corrosion, caustic stress corrosion cracking, chloride stress corrosion cracking
Small-bore branches near pumps and compressorsMechanical fatigue, including vibration-induced fatigue
Insulated, buried and dock pipingCorrosion under insulation, soil corrosion, atmospheric corrosion, galvanic corrosion, microbiologically influenced corrosion

Treat the table as a study map, not a description of any particular Bayway line; which mechanisms are active in a given circuit is for the owner's corrosion and inspection staff to establish.

No piping register: what drives a New Jersey piping programme

New Jersey registers vessels but not process piping. N.J.A.C. 12:90 covers boilers, unfired pressure vessels, refrigeration systems and pressure relief valves, and in-service process piping is not one of its equipment classes. A North Jersey piping programme rests on other foundations:

  • Federal mechanical integrity. The process safety and risk management rules list piping systems, valves included, as covered equipment. Under 40 CFR 68.73, inspection and testing follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, at a frequency consistent with manufacturers' recommendations and good engineering practice and more often if operating experience calls for it, and each inspection is documented with its date, the inspector, the equipment identifier, a description and the results.
  • New Jersey's Toxic Catastrophe Prevention Act program. For covered processes, N.J.A.C. 7:31-4.5 applies on top of 68.73 and asks for a record system of inspections, breakdowns, repairs and replacements of equipment handling extraordinarily hazardous substances, with the means to retrieve and analyse that data to set inspection frequencies.
  • Owner standards. Refiners and chemical companies commonly adopt API 570 in their own procedures as the in-service piping practice they follow, which is why employers value the certificate even though no state law names it for piping.

Dock lines, tank-farm headers and where API 570 stops

Harbor terminals are piping-heavy in another way. IMTT's Bayonne terminal lists seven deepwater ship berths and eleven barge berths, with connections to the Buckeye, Colonial and Harbor Pipeline systems. Kinder Morgan's Carteret terminal sheet lists six docks on the Arthur Kill, vessel loading at up to 30,000 barrels an hour, receipts from Colonial lines L6 and L7 and deliveries into Buckeye lines 801 and 1601. Colonial, owned outright by Brookfield since its former co-owners completed their sales in 2025, makes terminal-to-terminal transfers in the harbor through its Linden Junction facility.

That mix raises a boundary question the exam does not ask but the job does. Interstate pipelines are regulated under 49 CFR Part 195, and where pipeline jurisdiction ends and terminal piping begins is a regulatory determination made facility by facility, not something API 570 decides. On the terminal side, dock headers, manifolds and tank-farm transfer lines are commonly managed as API 570 circuits, with the usual questions about class, CML placement and interval. Know the code, and ask the operator where its boundary sits.

Many harbor sites sit on low ground beside tidal water, so lines that dip below grade, cross under roads or rise out of the soil near tank dikes are classic places for soil corrosion and microbiologically influenced corrosion, both listed on the Body of Knowledge. Salt-laden air at the docks drives atmospheric corrosion of bare pipe and supports, and dissimilar metals at hose stations and flanged connections invite galvanic corrosion.

CUI where salt air meets a North Jersey winter

Corrosion under insulation is the mechanism candidates from this region most often underestimate. Coastal moisture gets into damaged jacketing, freeze-thaw cycles open seams and crack mastic, and steam-traced or intermittently heated lines, common where terminal sheets list product heating as a service, spend long periods in the temperature range where wet insulation does the most damage. Cold lines that sweat in summer add a different pattern.

API 570 asks the owner to identify piping susceptible to CUI and to examine a share of it that depends on the piping class, with closer attention to locations such as penetrations, damaged jacketing, supports and low points. The exam takes those details from the code text, so learn them from the fifth edition on your effectivity sheet; study notes written for an older edition are a common source of wrong answers. What matters most is the reasoning: classify the line, find the susceptible locations, then choose between visual examination, profile radiography, guided wave screening and insulation removal.

Injection points and dead legs on sites that have changed purpose

Refineries inject wash water, neutralisers and corrosion inhibitors into overhead and effluent systems, and API 570 treats each injection point as a circuit of its own, with defined zones upstream and downstream for closer examination. The zone limits and the recommended inspection approach are set out in the current edition of API 570, and the exam can ask for them, so take them from the text rather than from a former employer's practice.

Dead legs are the other perennial topic, and North Jersey has a good supply because several harbor terminals stand on old refinery ground. The EPA's 2022 profile of the Perth Amboy site dates refinery operations and waste management there from 1920 to 1983, and describes the 260-acre property, bought by Buckeye from Chevron in 2012, as a major gasoline storage and blending site with about 4.4 million barrels of capacity. Conversions like that leave branches, bypasses and abandoned connections that no longer see flow. API 570 expects them to be identified, monitored while they remain and removed or isolated once they serve no purpose, and the 2027 Body of Knowledge asks for the minimum thickness of permanent blanks under B31.3, which is how many dead legs are finally retired.

Worked example: a dock transfer line from design to the next thickness survey

Given: an NPS 10 seamless carbon steel line (outside diameter 10.75 in, nominal wall 0.365 in) carrying diesel from a tank manifold to a dock; design pressure 150 psig at an ambient design temperature; B31.3 allowable stress S = 20,000 psi; quality factor E = 1.0 for seamless pipe; weld joint strength reduction factor W = 1.0; Y = 0.4. The owner's procedure sets a structural minimum of 0.10 in for this size, the thinnest CML reading is 0.240 in and the long-term corrosion rate is 0.008 in per year.

Pressure design thickness. B31.3 gives t = PD / [2(SEW + PY)] = (150 × 10.75) / [2(20,000 + 60)] = 1,612.5 / 40,120 = 0.040 in.

Which minimum governs. The 0.10 in structural minimum is larger than the 0.040 in pressure thickness, so it is the retirement thickness for this line. Large, low-pressure terminal lines are usually governed this way, which is why API 570 and RP 574 make you consider structural minimums rather than pressure alone.

Remaining life and interval. (0.240 − 0.10) / 0.008 = 17.5 years. The thickness inspection interval is half the remaining life, 8.75 years, unless the maximum API 570 sets for the line's class is shorter, in which case the class maximum applies. The owner assigns the class; check the maximum the current table gives for it before you answer.

Test pressure after a repair. At an ambient design temperature the B31.3 hydrostatic test pressure is 1.5 × 150 = 225 psig. The Class 150 flanges, rated at 285 psig at 100°F for Group 1.1 materials in B16.5, are comfortable at the 150 psig design condition, but in the exam check every component inside the test boundary before you accept a test pressure.

Winter adds one more check from the 2027 calculation list: B31.3's impact testing exemptions at the minimum design metal temperature, which decide whether a replacement spool for an exposed dock line needs Charpy testing.

From North Jersey piping work to API 570 eligibility

API looks at education and in-service piping experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency. A high school graduate needs three years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of piping, one of them supervising or performing inspection; a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology needs two; a BS needs one year of inspection activity.

  • Pipefitters and pipe welders on refinery and terminal work bring construction and repair years; the inspection year usually comes from moving into QA/QC or an owner's inspection group.
  • UT technicians taking CML readings for an inspection contractor are already doing core API 570 work, because thickness monitoring is how circuits are managed. If you need the method qualification first, see NDT training for Newark candidates.
  • Operators and maintenance planners earn operation and repair time but need the inspection year on top.
  • Engineers on the degree route need a year of supervising or performing inspection, often gained in an inspection department rotation.

The API 570 certification page sets out the rules in full, including credit for technical military service.

Keeping B31.3 study moving through a harbor year

B31.3 is the document that most often slows API 570 candidates, because the open-book half rewards knowing where things are in a long code. A sequence that copes with shift work:

  1. Read API 570 through, then RP 574 and the fifteen RP 571 paragraphs, asking the instructor about anything that does not match what you see on site.
  2. Work the calculation list: corrosion rates and intervals, quality factors, pressure design thickness and corroded MAWP, hydrostatic and pneumatic tests, impact testing, preheat and heat treatment, thermal expansion, B16.5 flange ratings and permanent blanks.
  3. Drill the B31.3 PDF: find a table, a definition or an exemption against the clock.
  4. Finish with timed papers that copy the closed-book and open-book split.

Refineries and terminals plan heavy work around product demand, so the quiet stretch differs from employer to employer; a self-paced course lets you push ahead in a slack month and keep ticking over during a turnaround.

Sponsoring piping inspectors from a terminal or refinery contractor

Terminal operators and inspection contractors in the harbor often need people who can carry both tank and piping work. Employers can enrol several API 570 candidates together, or mix API 570 and API 653 candidates, on one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually and sits the exam in their own window. A site building a CML programme after a conversion may need the people taking readings and the person signing circuits trained differently, and Atlantis can quote NDT method training and API exam prep together.

faq.q: Can I prepare for API 570 in Newark without attending a class?
faq.a: Yes. The course is self-paced online study with instructor Q&A, so you work from home or between shifts and send questions whenever a clause or calculation stops you. Nothing is held in a room in Newark. On exam day you sit the test in person at a Prometric test centre; Prometric lists test centres in and around Newark, and you pick one when you schedule within API's window.

faq.q: Are the dock lines at a Bayonne or Carteret terminal API 570 piping?
faq.a: Often they are managed that way. Dock headers, manifolds and transfer lines inside a terminal are commonly treated as in-service process piping and inspected to API 570 under the owner's programme. Lines that are part of a regulated pipeline fall under 49 CFR Part 195 instead, and the boundary between the two is a regulatory determination for each facility. For the exam you only need API 570 and the publications on your effectivity sheet.

faq.q: Is the Colonial pipeline at Linden covered by API 570?
faq.a: No. Colonial's system is an interstate hazardous liquid pipeline regulated by PHMSA under 49 CFR Part 195, not process piping. API 570 applies to in-service piping in refineries, chemical plants and similar facilities. Where terminal piping connects to a pipeline, the boundary between the two regimes is settled facility by facility under the federal rules, and an inspector should know which side of that line a circuit sits on before assigning it a class or an interval.

faq.q: Does New Jersey's boiler and pressure vessel bureau inspect process piping?
faq.a: No. N.J.A.C. 12:90 covers boilers, unfired pressure vessels, refrigeration systems and pressure relief valves, and process piping is not one of its equipment classes. Piping integrity in New Jersey plants is driven by the federal mechanical integrity rules, the state Toxic Catastrophe Prevention Act program for covered processes, and owner procedures that usually adopt API 570.

faq.q: Does winter change how CUI and cold service appear on the exam?
faq.a: The exam does not ask about New Jersey weather, but two topics come close. API 570's CUI provisions ask you to identify susceptible piping and the extent of examination by class, and B31.3's impact testing exemptions decide whether materials need Charpy testing at the minimum design metal temperature. Both are on the 2027 Body of Knowledge, and both are easier to remember if you picture an exposed dock line in January.

faq.q: I take UT thickness readings for a contractor in Linden. Does that count toward API 570?
faq.a: Thickness monitoring of piping circuits is inspection activity, so it can count if you do it while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. The time you need depends on your education: one year with a BS in engineering or technology, two with a two-year degree, three with a high school diploma, five or more with no formal education. Describe the work accurately on the application; API verifies it and decides.

faq.q: Should a Newark inspector take API 570 or API 510 first?
faq.a: Follow your experience. Terminal and pipe-rack work usually makes API 570 the faster route, because your years of piping experience count directly, while a candidate whose work is mostly columns and drums will qualify for API 510 sooner. Refinery inspection departments usually want both in time. See the API 510 exam-prep course if vessels are your main work.
